articles.title: Italy’s Green Bond Sees Demand Top $129 Billion in Global Orders
articles.summary:
Italy has raised approximately $9.4 billion through a new sovereign green bond, drawing more than $129 billion in investor orders as demand for the country’s sustainable debt far exceeded supply. […]
The post Italy’s Green Bond Sees Demand Top $129 Billion in Global Orders appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Italy’s Green Bond Sees Demand Top $129 Billion in Global Orders
- Italy raised approximately $9.4 billion through a new 12-year sovereign green bond, attracting an order book above $129 billion.
- Demand exceeded the issuance by more than 13 times, with over 330 investors across 35 countries and foreign buyers taking roughly 75% of the placement.
- Around 80% of the allocation went to ESG investors, with proceeds directed across six environmental categories under Italy’s updated Green Bond Framework.
Italy has raised approximately $9.4 billion through a new sovereign green bond, drawing more than $129 billion in investor orders as demand for the country’s sustainable debt far exceeded supply.
The Ministry of Economy and Finance completed the placement of the new BTP Green, which matures on October 30, 2038. The bond carries a 4.40% annual coupon, paid semi-annually, and was issued at a re-offer price of 99.591. That is equivalent to a gross annual yield of 4.492%.
The 12-year offering was more than 13 times oversubscribed. More than 330 investors from 35 countries participated, according to the ministry.
International demand was particularly strong. Foreign investors accounted for approximately 75% of the placement, while ESG-focused investors represented about 80%.
The figures give Italy a substantial pool of dedicated sustainable-finance demand as it channels sovereign borrowing toward its environmental spending priorities.
Green capital targets buildings and transport
Proceeds will be allocated under Italy’s Green Bond Framework, which was updated in late 2025. The framework establishes the criteria used to identify eligible environmental expenditure and report how green bond capital is deployed.
It defines six eligible categories: renewable energy, energy efficiency, clean transport, climate and environmental resilience, environmental protection, water and biodiversity, and environmental research.
Funds from the latest bond will be distributed across all six categories. However, the largest components are expected to support energy-efficiency measures for buildings and clean transport.
Those areas sit at the intersection of Italy’s climate commitments and its infrastructure investment requirements. Buildings remain a major source of European energy demand, while transport decarbonisation requires sustained investment in lower-emission infrastructure and mobility.
For investors, the framework provides the governance structure linking sovereign borrowing with identifiable environmental expenditure. Reporting against those categories will remain important as asset owners face greater scrutiny over the credibility and measurable impact of sustainable investments.
RELATED ARTICLE: Italy’s Rice Belt Faces $116M Drought Loss
Global investors drive demand
The size and geographic spread of the order book highlight continued institutional appetite for sovereign green debt despite a higher interest-rate environment.
The transaction attracted investors from 35 countries, giving Italy access to capital well beyond its domestic buyer base. The roughly 80% allocation to ESG investors also suggests the green designation brought a substantial pool of sustainability-focused capital into the transaction.
The bond was placed through a syndicate of six lead managers: Barclays Bank Ireland, BNP Paribas, Deutsche Bank, Intesa Sanpaolo, J.P. Morgan and Société Générale. Other specialists in Italian government bonds participated as co-lead managers.
Settlement was scheduled for September 29, 2026, the same date as the bond’s accrual date.
What investors should watch
Italy’s issuance adds another large sovereign transaction to the European green bond market at a time when governments face competing demands for climate investment, infrastructure spending and fiscal discipline.
For institutional investors, the scale of demand is notable. Orders exceeded the amount available by more than $119 billion, giving the Italian government significant depth in the market for labelled sovereign debt.
The longer-term test will be how effectively proceeds translate into measurable environmental outcomes. Allocation and impact reporting under the updated framework will therefore be central to investor assessment of the programme.
For governments elsewhere, Italy’s placement also illustrates the financing capacity available when sovereign debt is tied to clearly defined environmental expenditure. With international investors providing three-quarters of demand, the transaction shows how national climate investment programmes can draw on a global capital base rather than domestic funding alone.
That connection between sovereign financing, environmental governance and international capital will remain increasingly important as countries seek to fund the infrastructure required for the energy transition.

articles.title: Schneider Electric Expands SME Decarbonization Program With Greenly
articles.summary:
Schneider Electric is expanding its Decarbonization Champion Program globally through a new partnership with carbon accounting platform Greenly. The initiative targets small and medium-sized enterprises across the electrical value chain. […]
The post Schneider Electric Expands SME Decarbonization Program With Greenly appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Schneider Electric Expands SME Decarbonization Program With Greenly
- Schneider Electric and Greenly are expanding the Decarbonization Champion Program globally to help SME partners measure and reduce emissions.
- Each participating partner can access more than $34,000 in annual program value, including carbon accounting tools, consulting and training.
- Early audits identified potential annual savings of more than $178,000 for one manufacturer, linking decarbonization directly with operational efficiency.
Schneider Electric is expanding its Decarbonization Champion Program globally through a new partnership with carbon accounting platform Greenly.
The initiative targets small and medium-sized enterprises across the electrical value chain. It will give partners access to emissions measurement tools, sustainability consulting and practical support for reducing energy use and operating costs.
The expanded program is Schneider Electric’s first sustainability initiative specifically dedicated to its SME partners. It comes as suppliers face greater pressure from large customers and regulators to provide reliable emissions data.
Building decarbonization capabilities across the supply chain
The Decarbonization Champion Program combines Greenly’s carbon accounting platform with support from Schneider Electric’s SE Advisory Services.
Participating businesses receive a structured roadmap for measuring, managing and reducing their emissions. Schneider Electric estimates that the package provides more than $34,000 in value per partner each year.
Companies gain access to Schneider Electric’s Sustainability and Energy Tech School for training on sustainability fundamentals. Greenly’s platform allows participants to measure, visualize, track and report Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions.
SE Advisory Services then provides remote audits and strategy workshops. Consultants also work with businesses to develop individual decarbonization roadmaps.
Partners can access selected Schneider Electric decarbonization technologies and financial incentives. Participating companies also receive co-branded recognition through the program.
The combination addresses a persistent challenge for smaller suppliers. Many SMEs face requests for environmental data but lack dedicated sustainability teams, carbon accounting systems or the resources available to larger corporations.
Early audits identify significant savings
Initial deployments in the Pacific region suggest the program could deliver financial benefits alongside emissions reductions.
SE Advisory Services audits identified more than $28,500 in potential annual savings for one participating contractor.
A Queensland-based manufacturer identified more than $178,000 in potential yearly savings. Opportunities included improving air system efficiency, shifting electricity loads and optimizing equipment.
The findings give Schneider Electric and Greenly a financial case for extending decarbonization support deeper into supply chains. For SMEs, lower emissions can increasingly overlap with reduced energy costs and stronger operational performance.
“This program reflects our commitment as an Energy Tech Partner to creating value across our partner ecosystem. Together with Greenly, we are helping our partners build the capabilities needed to meet evolving market expectations, improve operational efficiency, and accelerate decarbonization,” said Bin Lu, Executive Vice President, Power Products, Schneider Electric. “By combining digital tools with expert guidance, we are enabling our partners to deliver long-term business value and sustainability impact.”
Regulation pushes emissions scrutiny deeper into supply chains
The program is expanding as sustainability reporting requirements increase pressure on companies to understand emissions beyond their own operations.
Large businesses increasingly require suppliers to provide emissions data and demonstrate progress against sustainability targets. That creates a knock-on effect for smaller companies throughout global value chains.
Regulatory developments are reinforcing that pressure. The European Union’s Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive has expanded corporate sustainability disclosure requirements, while Australia’s climate-related financial reporting regime is bringing mandatory climate disclosures into the market.
For panel builders, contractors and system integrators, the result is a changing competitive environment. Carbon measurement capabilities can influence procurement requirements and relationships with larger customers, even where an SME does not face the same direct reporting obligations.
RELATED ARTICLE: Schneider Electric Progresses on 2030 Sustainability Goals
Alexis Normand, CEO and co-founder of Greenly added: “Many SMEs want to act on carbon reduction but lack accessible tools and guidance. By combining software with hands-on support, we aim to make decarbonization both measurable and actionable across supply chains.”
From reporting requirement to business value
Schneider Electric is now rolling out the program globally through its partner ecosystem.
The approach reflects a broader shift in corporate decarbonization strategies. Large companies cannot address value-chain emissions solely through internal operational changes. Progress increasingly depends on suppliers having the data, technology and expertise needed to participate.
For executives and investors, the early savings identified through the program are particularly relevant. They show how emissions reduction initiatives can uncover operational efficiencies rather than functioning purely as a compliance expense.
As climate disclosure and customer expectations extend further into global supply chains, SMEs are becoming an increasingly important part of corporate transition strategies. Programs that combine carbon measurement with tangible cost reductions could help determine how quickly those smaller businesses can respond.

articles.title: Salesforce Backed Deal Brings Cowboy Clean Fuels Into Carbon Removal Market
articles.summary:
Cowboy Clean Fuels has entered the durable carbon removal market with its first credit sale, adding a new revenue stream alongside its renewable natural gas business. The credits were purchased […]
The post Salesforce Backed Deal Brings Cowboy Clean Fuels Into Carbon Removal Market appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Salesforce Backed Deal Brings Cowboy Clean Fuels Into Carbon Removal Market
- Cowboy Clean Fuels has completed its first durable carbon removal credit sale through a Salesforce-backed purchase facilitated by Milkywire, with delivery scheduled for 2026.
- The Wyoming company combines permanent carbon storage with renewable natural gas production using agricultural residues and depleted coalbed methane reservoirs.
- The purchase contributes to Salesforce’s commitment to contract $100 million of durable carbon removal by 2030.
Cowboy Clean Fuels has entered the durable carbon removal market with its first credit sale, adding a new revenue stream alongside its renewable natural gas business.
The credits were purchased through Milkywire as part of a Salesforce-backed carbon removal procurement, with delivery expected in 2026. The transaction puts Cowboy Clean Fuels into a growing market for engineered and nature-based solutions designed to store carbon for extended periods.
For the Wyoming-based company, the commercial model rests on an unusual combination. Its process uses agricultural waste, existing energy infrastructure and underground coal formations to produce renewable gas while permanently storing carbon dioxide.
Turning Wyoming’s subsurface into carbon storage
Cowboy Clean Fuels operates a biomass carbon removal and storage, or BiCRS, pathway in Wyoming’s Powder River Basin.
Agricultural processing residues are injected into depleted coalbed methane reservoirs. Indigenous microorganisms then anaerobically digest the biomass, producing renewable natural gas.
At the same time, carbon dioxide is absorbed onto underground coal surfaces and stored. Cowboy Clean Fuels says the resulting carbon removal has permanence exceeding 100 years.
The company quantifies removals through its patented BiCRS+RNG methodology, which was developed to ISO 14064-2:2019.
Projects are certified under the Absolute Carbon Standard developed by Absolute Climate. Credits are issued through Evident’s C-Capsule registry. Climate Vault Solutions has also independently assessed Cowboy Clean Fuels’ Triangle Unit project following a multi-phase technical review.
The model is designed to take advantage of infrastructure already embedded across the Powder River Basin. Its coalbed methane network and extensive inventory of unmineable coal seams provide potential capacity for both geological storage and renewable gas production.
“Durable carbon removal needs pathways that can be verified today and expanded tomorrow, and Wyoming’s subsurface gives us both. Buyers working with us get permanent removal alongside carbon-neutral renewable gas from the same operations, a combination very few suppliers can offer. This is an important step for Cowboy Clean Fuels and for the rural communities in Campbell County, Wyoming, that make the work possible.” said Ryan Waddington, Chief Executive Officer, Cowboy Clean Fuels
RELATED ARTICLE: Salesforce Accelerates Energy Transition with New $25 million Climate Investment
Salesforce procurement adds corporate demand
The purchase forms part of Salesforce’s pledge to contract $100 million in durable carbon removal by 2030.
Corporate procurement has become an important source of early demand for emerging carbon removal technologies. For suppliers, these purchases can provide commercial validation while technologies and project portfolios move toward greater scale.
Cowboy Clean Fuels is also developing additional projects across the Powder River Basin. The company is currently contracting both durable carbon removal volumes and carbon-neutral RNG supply.
Verified credits are listed on a registry and available for purchase.
Carbon removal meets legacy energy infrastructure
The Wyoming location adds another dimension to the project. Rather than building an entirely new industrial ecosystem, Cowboy Clean Fuels is using existing coalbed methane infrastructure and regional energy expertise.
That approach could provide new economic uses for legacy energy assets while supporting skilled employment in Campbell County. It also creates additional potential revenue streams around infrastructure already operating in the region.
For Wyoming, the model connects carbon management with an established energy workforce. That could become increasingly relevant as traditional energy-producing regions look for ways to participate in emerging low-carbon markets without abandoning existing industrial capabilities.
For corporate carbon buyers and investors, verification and durability will remain central considerations. Carbon removal procurement is increasingly focused on whether projects can demonstrate measurable storage, credible accounting and long-term permanence.
Cowboy Clean Fuels is positioning its BiCRS pathway around those requirements while pairing removal credits with renewable gas production.
If the model expands across the Powder River Basin, Wyoming’s legacy energy infrastructure could gain a new role in the US carbon management economy. The project also illustrates how durable removal markets may develop alongside existing energy industries rather than entirely outside them.

articles.title: Moeve, Emerita Bring Renewable Diesel to Spanish Mining in Industry First
articles.summary:
Spain targets mining emissions with renewable diesel Moeve and Emerita Resources are bringing renewable diesel into Spanish mining at industrial scale, targeting one of the harder areas of heavy industry […]
The post Moeve, Emerita Bring Renewable Diesel to Spanish Mining in Industry First appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Moeve, Emerita Bring Renewable Diesel to Spanish Mining in Industry First
- Moeve and Emerita Resources have signed Spain’s first agreement to deploy 100% renewable diesel, or HVO, at industrial scale in the mining sector.
- The fuel is expected to cut around 2,600 metric tons of CO2 emissions annually at Emerita’s Iberian Belt West project in Huelva.
- Moeve and Apical are investing $1.36 billion in a new Huelva biofuels plant with capacity for 500,000 metric tons of HVO and sustainable aviation fuel annually.
Spain targets mining emissions with renewable diesel
Moeve and Emerita Resources are bringing renewable diesel into Spanish mining at industrial scale, targeting one of the harder areas of heavy industry to decarbonize.
Under the agreement, Moeve will become the preferred supplier of hydrotreated vegetable oil, or HVO, to Emerita’s Iberian Belt West mining project in Huelva. The companies said it is the first agreement of its kind in Spain.
The second-generation biofuel can reduce lifecycle CO2 emissions by up to 90% compared with conventional diesel. Crucially for mining operators, HVO can also be used in existing diesel engines. That allows companies to reduce emissions without immediately replacing heavy equipment or transport fleets.
Moeve produces the fuel at its Palos de la Frontera facility in Huelva.
At Iberian Belt West, it will power heavy machinery during construction and subsequent mining operations. It will also be used for heavy-duty transport of mineral concentrates.
The companies estimate the switch could avoid around 2,600 metric tons of CO2 emissions each year. They compare that reduction with the annual carbon absorption of approximately 170,000 trees.
An immediate option for hard-to-electrify operations
Mining faces a difficult decarbonization challenge because its operations depend heavily on energy-intensive machinery and long-distance transport. Electrification can reduce emissions in some applications, but technical and infrastructure constraints remain for heavy equipment.
Renewable diesel offers operators an alternative that can be deployed using existing engines and distribution infrastructure.
“Accelerating the decarbonization of heavy industry is one of Moeve’s key strategic priorities, and to achieve this, we need forward-thinking partners. The agreement reached with Emerita demonstrates that the energy transition can go hand in hand with competitiveness by leveraging 2G biofuels as an immediate solution for the decarbonization of sectors that are difficult to electrify.” Carlos Barrasa, executive vice president of Commercial & Clean Energies at Moeve.
RELATED ARTICLE: Moeve Starts $1.2 Billion Green Hydrogen Project
Emerita CEO Joaquin Merino said the agreement is “fully aligned with Emerita’s environmental DNA.” He added that the Huelva development “is the ideal partner for this Moeve project as an example of sustainable mining.”
For mining executives, the project offers a practical case study in reducing operational emissions without waiting for full fleet electrification. It also places greater attention on lifecycle emissions, fuel sourcing and the availability of lower-carbon alternatives within industrial supply chains.
Huelva builds a local low-carbon industrial ecosystem
The partnership also has a regional industrial dimension. Renewable fuel production, mining operations and mineral export infrastructure are all located within Huelva.
That proximity could reduce logistical complexity while creating a more integrated value chain between energy production, resource extraction and exports.
Moeve is expanding that local supply base further. Together with partner Apical, the company is developing a new second-generation biofuels plant in Huelva.
The project carries a cumulative investment of $1.36 billion and is expected to provide flexible annual production capacity of 500,000 metric tons of HVO and sustainable aviation fuel.
Once operational, the facility will form part of what Moeve describes as the largest second-generation biofuels complex in southern Europe. It supports the company’s ambition to reach 2.5 million metric tons of annual biofuel production capacity by 2030 and lead the Iberian market.
For investors and industrial operators, the Huelva model illustrates how decarbonization investment can increasingly intersect with regional industrial strategy. Local fuel production can support mining and transport operations while reducing dependence on conventional fossil diesel.
The broader significance extends beyond Spain. Mining remains central to supplying minerals required for infrastructure and the energy transition itself. Reducing the operational footprint of extraction will therefore remain a key ESG challenge as demand for those materials grows.
Huelva’s emerging cluster provides one approach: combine local renewable fuel production with heavy industrial demand and existing export infrastructure. If the model proves commercially competitive at scale, it could offer a pathway for other mining regions where electrification remains technically or economically difficult.

articles.title: EIB, BNP Paribas Back $794 Million Guarantee Plan for EU Power Grids
articles.summary:
The European Investment Bank and BNP Paribas are expanding financing support for Europe’s electricity grids as the region confronts rising demand for infrastructure needed to electrify its economy. Under a […]
The post EIB, BNP Paribas Back $794 Million Guarantee Plan for EU Power Grids appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
EIB, BNP Paribas Back $794 Million Guarantee Plan for EU Power Grids
- EIB and BNP Paribas will build a guarantee portfolio of up to $794 million to support European electricity grid component manufacturers.
- The risk-sharing structure is expected to unlock as much as $3.18 billion in real-economy investment across the European Union.
- The deal forms part of the EIB’s $1.70 billion Pan-EU Power Grid package, backed by the EU’s InvestEU programme.
The European Investment Bank and BNP Paribas are expanding financing support for Europe’s electricity grids as the region confronts rising demand for infrastructure needed to electrify its economy.
Under a new agreement, the EIB will provide up to $397 million in counter-guarantees. BNP Paribas will commit an equivalent amount. Together, the institutions will create a bank guarantee portfolio worth up to $794 million for manufacturers supplying electricity grid equipment.
The financing structure is expected to mobilise up to $3.18 billion in investment in the real economy.
The agreement targets a growing bottleneck in Europe’s energy transition. Expanding renewable generation and electrifying transport, buildings and industry require substantial investment in transmission and distribution networks. Manufacturers must also expand production of the equipment needed to build them.
Financing Europe’s grid supply chain
The risk-sharing structure will increase BNP Paribas’ capacity to provide guarantees to European manufacturers of critical grid components. These guarantees can help companies secure contracts, expand production and respond to growing orders without placing the full financing burden on their balance sheets.
For the EIB, the agreement links infrastructure investment with industrial competitiveness and energy security.
EIB Vice-President Ambroise Fayolle said: “We are pleased to continue our cooperation with BNP Paribas on Europe’s energy security and green transition. Following our agreement on wind energy last year, we have now concluded a risk-sharing agreement to support companies manufacturing the equipment essential for developing energy grids. In 2025, the EIB Group invested $37.42 billion in energy worldwide, including $13.15 billion in grids and storage. In 2026, we are continuing this commitment with the same level of ambition.”
The EIB’s 2025 figures are equivalent to approximately $37.42 billion in global energy investment, including about $13.15 billion for grids and storage.
Rodolfe Vergeaud, Co-Head of Transaction Banking, Head of Trade and Working Capital BNP Paribas CIB EMEA, said: “Strengthening Europe’s electricity grids requires mobilising all players throughout the value chain. This agreement with the EIB enables us to go further in supporting manufacturers of essential electricity grid components by increasing our capacity to meet their guarantee needs and support their development.”
RELATED ARTICLE: EIB Invests $46 Million in Modular Nuclear
EU financing shifts toward grid capacity
The agreement sits within the EIB’s $1.70 billion Pan-EU Power Grid package, which is dedicated to developing, modernising and strengthening electricity networks across the bloc. The initiative receives support from the European Union’s InvestEU programme.
It follows a broader EIB push to finance the infrastructure and manufacturing capacity behind Europe’s energy transition.
The bank previously made approximately $7.37 billion available for wind energy. BNP Paribas also participates in that initiative. The two institutions signed an agreement in February 2025 covering a guarantee portfolio equivalent to about $1.13 billion.
The latest transaction shifts attention further into the grid infrastructure needed to connect new generation capacity and manage changing electricity flows.
Grid investment becomes an industrial priority
For investors and corporate leaders, Europe’s grid expansion is increasingly both an infrastructure challenge and a supply-chain issue.
Capital for renewable generation alone cannot deliver Europe’s energy transition if grid connections, transmission capacity and equipment manufacturing fail to keep pace. Financing mechanisms that reduce risk for suppliers can therefore influence how quickly planned infrastructure moves from development into construction.
The EIB and BNP Paribas structure also shows how public guarantees can be used to draw commercial banking capacity into strategic sectors without relying solely on direct public investment.
For the European Union, that financing model serves several priorities at once. It supports electrification, strengthens domestic manufacturing capacity and reduces infrastructure constraints that could slow renewable deployment.
As electricity demand grows and Europe pursues greater energy security, the ability to finance the companies building the grid itself is becoming central to the region’s climate and industrial strategy.

articles.summary:
Primark has signed a long-term purchase agreement with textile recycling company Circ to bring textile-to-textile recycled polyester into its clothing from 2029. The agreement is Primark’s first multi-year offtake deal […]
The post Primark Signs Long Term Circ Deal to Scale Textile-to-Textile Recycling appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Primark Signs Long Term Circ Deal to Scale Textile-to-Textile Recycling
- Primark has signed its first multi-year offtake agreement with a textile-to-textile recycler, securing recycled polyester from Circ for clothing from 2029.
- Circ will supply material from its first industrial-scale recycling facility, using post-consumer and post-industrial textile waste sourced globally.
- The agreement targets one of fashion’s toughest circularity challenges: recycling polycotton blends while reducing dependence on virgin polyester.
Primark has signed a long-term purchase agreement with textile recycling company Circ to bring textile-to-textile recycled polyester into its clothing from 2029.
The agreement is Primark’s first multi-year offtake deal with a textile-to-textile recycler. It gives Circ a major commercial customer as it works to move its recycling technology into industrial-scale production.
For Primark, the partnership is intended to expand access to circular materials without abandoning the affordability at the centre of its business model. It also supports the retailer’s efforts to reduce its reliance on virgin polyester.
From textile waste back into clothing
Circ has developed technology to tackle polycotton, a blend of polyester and cotton that is widely used across the global apparel sector but difficult to recycle.
Its patented process separates polyester from cellulose in blended textile waste. Both components can then be recovered and converted into materials suitable for use in new clothing.
Under the agreement, recycled polyester will be produced at Circ’s commercial facility. The site will support the company’s move into industrial-scale textile-to-textile recycling.
Feedstock will include both post-consumer and post-industrial textile waste. Circ plans to source those materials globally, including through the recovery of textile waste generated in Europe.
“This partnership with Primark represents exactly the kind of long-term commercial commitment needed to move textile-to-textile recycling from innovation to industry standard,” said Peter Majeranowski, CEO of Circ. “When a global fashion retailer commits to integrating recycled materials into future collections, it sends a powerful signal across the industry: the demand is here, the materials are ready, and the opportunity to scale circular material supply chains is real.”
Primark pushes circularity deeper into its supply chain
The agreement sits within Primark’s wider Primark Cares strategy, which includes efforts to extend product life, reduce waste and increase the use of recycled fibres.
The retailer has also introduced a Circular Product Standard to incorporate circular design principles into product development. Other initiatives focus on reuse and repair, with the aim of keeping clothing in use for longer.
For a value retailer operating at significant scale, the challenge is not simply gaining access to new recycled materials. Those materials must also be available in sufficient volumes and at costs compatible with mass-market clothing.
RELATED ARTICLE: Fast-fashion chain Primark expands sustainable cotton programme
Lynne Walker, Director of Primark Cares said: “We launched Primark Cares with a focus on improving the quality and longevity of our clothing, and in the process show that clothes made to last longer don’t have to come at a higher price. Since then, we’ve delivered tangible progress, including increasing the use of recycled fibres, introducing products designed to be recycled and enhancing traceability across our supply chain. This partnership is an important milestone in accelerating our ambitions to further embed circularity in our business and help scale innovative textile-to-textile recycling solutions that could play a transformational role in the future of fashion.”
Why long-term purchasing matters for textile recycling
For investors and fashion executives, the structure of the agreement is as important as the material itself.
Textile-to-textile recycling technologies require significant capital to move from demonstration projects into commercial production. Long-term purchase commitments can provide recyclers with greater demand visibility as they finance and develop larger facilities.
They can also help fashion groups secure access to emerging recycled materials as regulation and corporate sustainability targets increase pressure on the industry to address waste and resource use.
The Circ-Primark agreement therefore connects two sides of fashion’s circularity challenge. Recyclers need dependable demand to justify industrial expansion, while retailers need reliable supplies of materials capable of replacing virgin inputs.
If commercial-scale facilities can deliver consistent quality, volume and competitive pricing, textile-to-textile recycling could become a more significant part of fashion supply chains. Primark’s planned introduction of Circ material in 2029 will provide a test of whether those technologies can move beyond limited collections and into mass-market clothing.

articles.full_text:
Shell Backs Major LNG Canada Expansion as Asian Gas Demand Rises
- LNG Canada Phase 2 will double production capacity from 14 million tonnes per annum (mtpa) to 28 mtpa, with commercial operations expected in the early 2030s.
- Shell holds a 40% interest in the project and expects to receive nearly 6 mtpa of additional LNG from the expansion.
- The project targets rising Asian demand as Shell forecasts global LNG consumption will climb around 65% from 2025 levels to nearly 700 mtpa by 2050.
Shell has taken a final investment decision on LNG Canada Phase 2, clearing the way for a major expansion of the British Columbia export facility.
The project will double LNG Canada’s production capacity to 28 mtpa. Two additional LNG processing trains will be built within the existing Kitimat facility, alongside expanded storage, loading and utility infrastructure.
Commercial operations are expected to begin in the early 2030s.
For Shell, the decision expands a strategic LNG position on Canada’s Pacific coast and provides greater access to Asian energy markets. The company owns 40% of LNG Canada and expects to receive nearly 6 mtpa of additional LNG from Phase 2.
“LNG Canada is a core part of our Integrated Gas portfolio, helping to supply LNG to customers in Asia at a time when diversity of energy supplies and energy security are increasingly important,” said Cederic Cremers, Shell’s Integrated Gas President. “Phase 2 supports Shell’s strategic objective to be the world’s leading integrated gas and LNG business by connecting Canadian resources with Shell’s global LNG portfolio, trading capability and customer reach.”
Building out Canada’s Pacific LNG corridor
LNG Canada is owned by Shell, PETRONAS, PetroChina, Mitsubishi Corporation and Korea Gas Corporation. Their respective interests are 40%, 25%, 15%, 15% and 5%.
The venture operates through an equity lifting structure. Each participant is responsible for taking its proportionate share of LNG production and supplying its share of feed gas.
Phase 2 will require infrastructure beyond the two additional processing trains. Plans include another LNG storage tank, condensate tank and loading berth, together with expanded utility and process systems.
Coastal GasLink will also increase capacity along its existing 670-kilometre pipeline. Five new compressor stations are planned to support the expansion.
The location gives LNG Canada direct Pacific access to Asian buyers. That reduces the distance to key markets compared with many LNG projects supplying Asia from the U.S. Gulf Coast.
RELATED ARTICLE: Shell Sells Sprng Energy to Aditya Birla for $1.8B
Shell targets long-term LNG demand growth
Shell expects global LNG demand to rise sharply over the coming decades. Its LNG Outlook 2026 projects demand increasing from 422 mtpa in 2025 to nearly 700 mtpa by 2050, a rise of about 65%.
The company expects growth to come from rising overall energy consumption and demand for flexible and reliable energy supplies. Meeting that outlook would require further investment in liquefaction capacity through the 2030s and 2040s.
Shell said the Phase 2 investment fits within its disciplined capital allocation framework. It expects the project to generate double-digit returns and an internal rate of return above the hurdle rate for its Integrated Gas business.
The expansion also aligns with Shell’s stated strategy of maintaining a leading integrated gas and LNG business through the 2040s.
Climate considerations remain central to LNG growth
The expansion comes as governments and investors continue to debate the long-term role of natural gas in the energy transition.
Shell points to LNG’s potential role in replacing higher-emitting coal in power generation. According to International Energy Agency data cited by the company, electricity generated from LNG has an average global life-cycle greenhouse gas emissions intensity around 40% below coal-fired electricity.
At the same time, new LNG infrastructure brings long investment horizons into a period of tightening climate targets. That places lifecycle emissions, methane management, project economics and future demand assumptions under greater scrutiny.
For executives and investors, LNG Canada Phase 2 reflects the scale of capital still moving into global gas infrastructure. It also highlights Canada’s growing role in connecting North American resources directly with Asia.
If Shell’s demand projections materialize, projects such as LNG Canada will form part of a much larger wave of liquefaction investment needed after 2030. The central question for markets will be how that growth develops alongside national climate commitments, evolving energy security priorities and the accelerating buildout of lower-carbon energy systems.
